title: Chapter 11: Testing, Evaluation, Monitoring, and Cost Control
content:
Chapter 11: Testing, Evaluation, Monitoring, and Cost Control

Opening Hook: A Real AI App Must Work More Than Once

An AI demo is easy to impress with.

You type one question. The model gives one good answer. Everyone says, “That’s amazing.”

But real users do not ask only one perfect question.

They ask vague questions. They paste messy text. They ask things outside the document. They ask for risky actions. They ask the same thing in different ways. They expect the app to be fast. They expect the answer to be useful. They expect the cost to stay under control.

A serious AI app is not finished when it works once.

It is ready when it works reliably across many messy inputs.

That is what this chapter is about.

You will build a simple evaluation system for AI agents.

It will help you test:

  • Whether outputs contain expected information
  • Whether the assistant avoids prohibited phrases
  • Whether responses follow required formats
  • Whether the app logs results
  • Whether costs and model calls are estimated
  • Whether failures are visible instead of hidden

This chapter turns you from an AI app builder into an AI app evaluator.

That is a major professional step.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this chapter, you will understand:

  • Why AI apps need evaluation
  • The difference between testing and evaluation
  • How to create basic evaluation datasets
  • How to score AI outputs with simple rules
  • How to test expected keywords and required sections
  • How to detect prohibited phrases
  • How to log agent behavior
  • How to track latency
  • How to estimate token usage and cost
  • How to debug RAG systems
  • How to evaluate tool-using agents
  • How to evaluate memory and workflow agents
  • How to create a simple evaluation report
  • How to improve AI apps based on test results

Why This Chapter Matters

Earlier chapters gave your AI applications power.

Chapter 4 gave your app documents. Chapter 6 gave your app tools. Chapter 7 gave your app memory. Chapter 8 gave your app workflow automation. Chapter 9 gave your app multi-step reasoning. Chapter 10 gave your app guardrails.

Now you need reliability.

Without evaluation, you are guessing.

You may think your app works because it gave a good answer once.

But you need to know:

Does it work on 10 questions?
Does it work on 100 questions?
Does it fail safely?
Does it admit uncertainty?
Does it follow the requested format?
Does it avoid risky claims?
Does it retrieve the right context?
Does it cost too much?

Testing and evaluation help you answer those questions.

11.1 Testing vs Evaluation

Testing and evaluation are related, but they are not exactly the same.

Testing

Testing checks whether normal code behaves correctly.

Example:

assert add_numbers(2, 3) == 5

Testing is great for deterministic logic.

You used tests in earlier chapters for:

  • Command parsing
  • Prompt generation
  • JSON parsing
  • Chunking
  • Memory storage
  • Guardrail detection
  • Task generation

These are predictable.

Evaluation

Evaluation checks whether AI output is good enough.

That is harder because model output can vary.

Example:

Question:
Explain RAG.

Expected behavior:
The answer should mention retrieval and generation.

The exact wording may change, but the core meaning should be present.

Evaluation is not always a simple pass/fail test.

Sometimes it is a score.

11.2 Why AI Evaluation Is Different

Traditional software usually gives predictable output.

If you write:

2 + 2

you expect:

4

AI output is different.

The same prompt may produce slightly different wording.

For example, this question:

What is RAG?

could produce:

RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

or:

RAG is a technique where an AI system retrieves relevant information before generating an answer.

Both are acceptable.

That means your evaluation should often check meaning, structure, safety, and usefulness rather than exact wording.

11.3 What Should You Evaluate?

A practical AI app should be evaluated across several dimensions.

DimensionQuestion
RelevanceDid the answer address the user’s request?
AccuracyWas the answer factually reasonable?
GroundingWas the answer based on provided context?
FormatDid the output follow the required format?
SafetyDid the response avoid risky advice or actions?
HelpfulnessWas the answer useful to the user?
CompletenessDid it include the important parts?
ConcisenessWas it too long or too vague?
LatencyWas it fast enough?
CostWas the model usage reasonable?
Failure handlingDid it fail clearly and safely?

You do not need a complex evaluation system at the beginning.

Start with simple checks.

Then improve.

11.4 The Evaluation Mindset

A good AI evaluator thinks like this:

What should this app do?
What should it refuse?
What should it say when it does not know?
What format should it return?
What mistakes are most likely?
How can I detect those mistakes?

Do not only test happy paths.

A happy path is a perfect input.

Example:

Summarize this clear paragraph.

Real users also create edge cases:

Summarize this 20-page messy document.

What does the PDF say about something not in the PDF?

Send this email without showing me.

Remember my API key.

Return JSON but include a long explanation too.

Evaluation should include messy inputs.

11.5 Project: AI Agent Evaluation Script

What This Project Does

This project creates a simple evaluation runner for an AI assistant.

It will:

  1. Load test cases from JSON
  2. Run each test case through an assistant function
  3. Check expected keywords
  4. Check prohibited phrases
  5. Check required sections
  6. Measure latency
  7. Estimate token usage and cost
  8. Save results to a Markdown report
  9. Show a pass/fail summary

Who This Helps

This project helps:

  • Developers testing AI assistants
  • Freelancers proving app quality to clients
  • Students creating stronger portfolio projects
  • Teams checking prompt changes
  • AI builders debugging RAG and agent behavior
  • Anyone who wants fewer surprises before deployment

What You Will Build

11.6 Setup

Step 1: Create the Folder

mkdir chapter_11_evaluation
cd chapter_11_evaluation
mkdir test_cases outputs

Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment

python -m venv .venv

Activate it.

On macOS or Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Step 3: Create requirements.txt

openai
python-dotenv

pytest

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Create .env.example

OPENAI_API_KEY=replace_with_your_api_key
OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini
OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2
ESTIMATED_INPUT_COST_PER_1K=0.00015
ESTIMATED_OUTPUT_COST_PER_1K=0.00060

Copy it to .env.

On macOS or Linux:

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Then edit .env and add your real API key.

Never publish your real .env file.

Pricing and model names may change. Check your provider’s current documentation and billing dashboard before publication or deployment.

11.9 File: llm_client.py

This chapter uses a reusable client with basic call metadata.

"""
Chapter 11: Reusable LLM Client with basic call tracking.
"""

import os from dataclasses import dataclass, field from dotenv import load_dotenv from openai import OpenAI

load_dotenv()

def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float:

"""Read a float from environment variables safely."""

raw_value = os.getenv(name)

if raw_value is None:
return default

try:

return float(raw_value)

except ValueError:
return default

@dataclass

class LLMConfig:

"""Configuration for the LLM client."""

model: str = field(
 default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini")
 )
 temperature: float = field(
 default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2)
 )

@dataclass

class LLMResponse:

"""Response text plus basic usage estimates."""

text: str
input_chars: int
output_chars: int
model: str

class LLMClient:

"""Small reusable client for sending prompts to an LLM."""

def __init__(self, config: LLMConfig | None = None):
 self.config = config or LLMConfig()
 api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")

if not api_key:
raise ValueError(
"OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file."
)

self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key)

def build_input(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""Build model input from system and user text."""

if not system.strip():
 raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.")
if not user.strip():
 raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.")

return f"""
System instruction:

{system.strip()}

User request:

{user.strip()}

"""

def complete_with_metadata(self, system: str, user: str) -> LLMResponse:
"""Send a request and return response with simple metadata."""

model_input = self.build_input(system=system, user=user)

response = self.client.responses.create(
model=self.config.model,
input=model_input,
temperature=self.config.temperature,
)

output_text = response.output_text

return LLMResponse(

text=output_text,
input_chars=len(model_input),
output_chars=len(output_text),
model=self.config.model,
)

def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""Send a request and return text only."""

return self.complete_with_metadata(system=system, user=user).text

11.10 File: assistant_under_test.py

This is a small assistant used for evaluation.

In a real project, you would replace this file with your actual assistant, RAG app, tool agent, or workflow agent.

"""
A simple assistant used for Chapter 11 evaluation.

In real projects, replace this with the app or agent you want to evaluate.
"""

from llm_client import LLMClient, LLMResponse

ASSISTANT_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a careful Python AI tutor and assistant.

Rules:
- Be clear and practical.
- Do not invent facts.
- Do not store secrets, API keys, passwords, or private tokens.
- If the user asks you to remember a secret, refuse and explain why.
- For task plans, include sections labeled Goal and Tasks.
- Avoid guarantees and unsupported certainty.
"""

def run_assistant(user_input: str) -> LLMResponse:

"""
Run the assistant under test.

Returns response text plus basic metadata.
"""

client = LLMClient()

return client.complete_with_metadata(

system=ASSISTANT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
user=user_input,
)

11.12 File: cost_tracker.py

This file estimates token count and cost.

Important: this is a rough estimate, not provider billing truth.

"""
Simple token and cost estimation helpers.

This is a rough estimate for learning purposes.
Check your provider dashboard for actual billed usage.
"""

import os from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

def estimate_tokens_from_chars(char_count: int) -> int:

"""
Estimate tokens from character count.

A common rough estimate is about 4 characters per token in English.
This is not exact.
"""

if char_count <= 0:
return 0

return max(1, round(char_count / 4))

def get_env_cost(name: str, default: float) -> float:

"""Read a cost value from environment variables."""

raw_value = os.getenv(name)

if raw_value is None:
return default

try:

return float(raw_value)

except ValueError:
return default

def estimate_cost(

input_tokens: int,
 output_tokens: int,
 input_cost_per_1k: float | None = None,
 output_cost_per_1k: float | None = None,
) -> float:
 """
 Estimate cost from token counts.

Costs are configured per 1,000 tokens.
"""

input_rate = input_cost_per_1k

if input_rate is None:
input_rate = get_env_cost("ESTIMATED_INPUT_COST_PER_1K", 0.00015)

output_rate = output_cost_per_1k

if output_rate is None:
output_rate = get_env_cost("ESTIMATED_OUTPUT_COST_PER_1K", 0.00060)

input_cost = (input_tokens / 1000) * input_rate
 output_cost = (output_tokens / 1000) * output_rate

return input_cost + output_cost

11.13 File: evaluators.py

This file checks AI outputs against simple rules.

"""
Evaluation helpers for AI assistant outputs.
"""

import json from pathlib import Path

from eval_models import EvalCase

def load_eval_cases(path: str) -> list[EvalCase]:

"""
Load evaluation cases from a JSON file.
"""

file_path = Path(path)

if not file_path.exists():
 raise FileNotFoundError(f"Evaluation file not found: {path}")

data = json.loads(file_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

if not isinstance(data, list):
raise ValueError("Evaluation file must contain a list of cases.")

cases = []

for item in data:
cases.append(
EvalCase(
id=str(item["id"]),
input=str(item["input"]),
expected_keywords=list(item.get("expected_keywords", [])),
prohibited_phrases=list(item.get("prohibited_phrases", [])),
required_sections=list(item.get("required_sections", [])),
notes=str(item.get("notes", "")),
)
)

return cases

def check_expected_keywords(output: str, keywords: list[str]) -> list[str]:

"""
Return missing expected keywords.
"""

lowered = output.lower()
 missing = []

for keyword in keywords:
if keyword.lower() not in lowered:
missing.append(keyword)

return missing

def check_prohibited_phrases(output: str, phrases: list[str]) -> list[str]:

"""
Return prohibited phrases found in output.
"""

lowered = output.lower()
 found = []

for phrase in phrases:
if phrase.lower() in lowered:
found.append(phrase)

return found

def check_required_sections(output: str, sections: list[str]) -> list[str]:

"""
Return required sections missing from output.
"""

lowered = output.lower()
 missing = []

for section in sections:
if section.lower() not in lowered:
missing.append(section)

return missing

def score_case(

output: str,
expected_keywords: list[str],
prohibited_phrases: list[str],
required_sections: list[str],
) -> tuple[float, list[str]]:
"""
Score one output using simple rule-based checks.

Returns:
(score, issues)
"""

issues = []
 total_checks = (
 len(expected_keywords)
 + len(prohibited_phrases)
 + len(required_sections)
 )

if total_checks == 0:
total_checks = 1

failed_checks = 0

missing_keywords = check_expected_keywords(output, expected_keywords)

for keyword in missing_keywords:
issues.append(f"missing_keyword:{keyword}")
failed_checks += 1

found_prohibited = check_prohibited_phrases(output, prohibited_phrases)

for phrase in found_prohibited:
issues.append(f"prohibited_phrase:{phrase}")
failed_checks += 1

missing_sections = check_required_sections(output, required_sections)

for section in missing_sections:
issues.append(f"missing_section:{section}")
failed_checks += 1

passed_checks = max(0, total_checks - failed_checks)
 score = passed_checks / total_checks

return score, issues

11.14 File: logger.py

This file logs evaluation events.

"""
Simple logging utility for Chapter 11 evaluation.
"""

from datetime import datetime from pathlib import Path

def log_event(message: str, log_path: str = "outputs/eval.log") -> None:

"""
Append an event to the evaluation log.

Avoid logging secrets or sensitive user data in production systems.
"""

path = Path(log_path)
path.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

with open(path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write(f"{datetime.now().isoformat()} - {message}\n")

11.15 File: report_writer.py

This file creates a Markdown report from evaluation results.

"""
Markdown report writer for Chapter 11 evaluation results.
"""

from pathlib import Path from datetime import datetime

from eval_models import EvalResult

def summarize_results(results: list[EvalResult]) -> dict:

"""
Summarize evaluation results.
"""

total = len(results)
 passed = sum(1 for result in results if result.passed)
 failed = total - passed
average_score = 0.0
 total_cost = 0.0
 total_latency = 0.0
if total:
 average_score = sum(result.score for result in results) / total
 total_cost = sum(result.estimated_cost for result in results)
 total_latency = sum(result.latency_seconds for result in results)

return {

"total": total,
"passed": passed,
"failed": failed,
"average_score": average_score,
"total_cost": total_cost,
"total_latency": total_latency,
}

def build_markdown_report(results: list[EvalResult]) -> str:

"""
Build a Markdown evaluation report.
"""

summary = summarize_results(results)

lines = [
"# AI Agent Evaluation Report",
"",
f"Generated: {datetime.now().isoformat()}",
"",
"## Summary",
"",
f"- Total cases: {summary['total']}",
f"- Passed: {summary['passed']}",
f"- Failed: {summary['failed']}",
f"- Average score: {summary['average_score']:.2f}",
f"- Total estimated cost: ${summary['total_cost']:.6f}",
f"- Total latency: {summary['total_latency']:.2f} seconds",
"",
"## Results",
"",
]

for result in results:
status = "PASS" if result.passed else "FAIL"

lines.extend(
[
f"### {result.case_id} — {status}",
"",
f"- Score: {result.score:.2f}",
f"- Latency: {result.latency_seconds:.2f} seconds",
f"- Estimated input tokens: {result.estimated_input_tokens}",
f"- Estimated output tokens: {result.estimated_output_tokens}",
f"- Estimated cost: ${result.estimated_cost:.6f}",
f"- Issues: {', '.join(result.issues) if result.issues else 'none'}",
"",
"**Input:**",
"",
"```text",
result.input,
"```",
"",
"**Output:**",
"",
"```text",
result.output,
"```",
"",
]
)

return "\n".join(lines)

def save_report(

results: list[EvalResult],
output_dir: str = "outputs",
) -> Path:
"""
Save evaluation report to Markdown.
"""

output_path = Path(output_dir)
output_path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
 file_path = output_path / f"evaluation_report_{timestamp}.md"

report = build_markdown_report(results)
file_path.write_text(report, encoding="utf-8")

return file_path

11.16 File: eval_runner.py

This file runs the full evaluation.

"""
Evaluation runner for Chapter 11.
"""

import time

from assistant_under_test import run_assistant from cost_tracker import estimate_tokens_from_chars, estimate_cost from eval_models import EvalResult from evaluators import load_eval_cases, score_case from logger import log_event from report_writer import save_report, summarize_results

def evaluate_case(case) -> EvalResult:

"""
Run and evaluate one test case.
"""

log_event(f"Starting case: {case.id}")

start_time = time.perf_counter()
 response = run_assistant(case.input)
 end_time = time.perf_counter()

latency = end_time - start_time

score, issues = score_case(
output=response.text,
expected_keywords=case.expected_keywords,
prohibited_phrases=case.prohibited_phrases,
required_sections=case.required_sections,
)

passed = score == 1.0

input_tokens = estimate_tokens_from_chars(response.input_chars)
 output_tokens = estimate_tokens_from_chars(response.output_chars)

estimated = estimate_cost(
input_tokens=input_tokens,
output_tokens=output_tokens,
)

result = EvalResult(
case_id=case.id,
passed=passed,
score=score,
input=case.input,
output=response.text,
issues=issues,
latency_seconds=latency,
input_chars=response.input_chars,
output_chars=response.output_chars,
estimated_input_tokens=input_tokens,
estimated_output_tokens=output_tokens,
estimated_cost=estimated,
)

log_event(f"Finished case: {case.id} | passed={passed} | score={score:.2f}")

return result

def run_evaluation(eval_file: str = "test_cases/basic_eval_cases.json") -> list[EvalResult]:

"""
Run all evaluation cases.
"""

cases = load_eval_cases(eval_file)
 results = []

for case in cases:
result = evaluate_case(case)
results.append(result)

return results

def main() -> None:

"""
Run evaluation and save report.
"""

print("\nAI Agent Evaluation Runner") print("=" * 45)

try:
 results = run_evaluation()
 summary = summarize_results(results)
 report_path = save_report(results)

print("\nSummary") print("-" * 45) print(f"Total cases: {summary['total']}") print(f"Passed: {summary['passed']}") print(f"Failed: {summary['failed']}") print(f"Average score: {summary['average_score']:.2f}") print(f"Total estimated cost: ${summary['total_cost']:.6f}") print(f"Total latency: {summary['total_latency']:.2f} seconds") print(f"\nReport saved to: {report_path}")

except Exception as error:

print(f"Evaluation failed: {error}")

if name == "main":

main()

import pytest

from evaluators import (

load_eval_cases,
check_expected_keywords,
check_prohibited_phrases,
check_required_sections,
score_case,
)

def test_check_expected_keywords():

output = "RAG uses retrieval and generation."

missing = check_expected_keywords(output, ["retrieval", "generation", "context"])

assert missing == ["context"]

def test_check_prohibited_phrases():

output = "I guarantee this is 100% accurate."

found = check_prohibited_phrases(output, ["guarantee", "100% accurate"])

assert "guarantee" in found
 assert "100% accurate" in found

def test_check_required_sections():

output = """
Goal:
Build a PDF chatbot.

Tasks:
1. Extract text.
2. Add retrieval.
"""

missing = check_required_sections(output, ["Goal", "Tasks", "Risks"])

assert missing == ["Risks"]

def test_score_case_passes():

score, issues = score_case(
output="RAG uses retrieval and generation.",
expected_keywords=["retrieval", "generation"],
prohibited_phrases=["I guarantee"],
required_sections=[],
)

assert score == 1.0
 assert issues == []

def test_score_case_fails():

score, issues = score_case(
output="RAG is useful. I guarantee success.",
expected_keywords=["retrieval"],
prohibited_phrases=["guarantee"],
required_sections=["Tasks"],
)

assert score < 1.0
 assert "missing_keyword:retrieval" in issues
 assert "prohibited_phrase:guarantee" in issues
 assert "missing_section:Tasks" in issues

def test_load_eval_cases(tmp_path: Path): eval_file = tmp_path / "cases.json"

eval_file.write_text(

json.dumps(

[
{
"id": "case_1",
"input": "Explain RAG.",
"expected_keywords": ["retrieval"],
"prohibited_phrases": ["guarantee"],
"required_sections": [],
"notes": "Test note",
}
]
),
encoding="utf-8",
)

cases = load_eval_cases(str(eval_file))

assert len(cases) == 1
 assert cases[0].id == "case_1"
 assert cases[0].input == "Explain RAG."

with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):

load_eval_cases("missing_file.json")

## Project: AI Agent Evaluation Script

This project builds a simple evaluation runner for AI assistants and agents.

## Features

- Loads test cases from JSON
- Runs an assistant against each case
- Checks expected keywords
- Checks prohibited phrases
- Checks required sections
- Measures latency
- Estimates token usage and cost
- Saves a Markdown evaluation report
- Includes non-API tests for evaluation logic

## Setup

python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

python -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 pip install -r requirements.txt Copy-Item .env.example .env

Edit `.env` and add your API key.

## Run Tests

pytest

## Run Evaluation

python eval_runner.py

## Output

Evaluation reports are saved in:

outputs/

Example:

outputs/evaluation_report_20260523_143000.md

## Important Notes

- Cost estimates are rough.
- Check your provider dashboard for actual usage.
- Evaluation rules are simple and should be expanded for real projects.
- AI output can vary, so avoid relying only on exact string matches.

11.21 How the Code Works

This project has six main parts.

Part 1: Evaluation Dataset

The JSON file contains test cases.

Each test case includes:

{

"id": "rag_definition",
"input": "Explain RAG in one paragraph.",
"expected_keywords": ["retrieval", "generation"],
"prohibited_phrases": ["I guarantee"],
"required_sections": [],
"notes": "The answer should mention retrieval and generation."
}

This makes your evaluation repeatable.

Instead of randomly testing prompts by hand, you build a test set.

Part 2: Assistant Under Test

The assistant_under_test.py file contains the app being evaluated.

For this chapter, it is a simple assistant.

In a real project, you can replace it with:

  • Your RAG assistant
  • Your tool-using agent
  • Your memory assistant
  • Your workflow automation app
  • Your multi-agent research workflow
  • Your final capstone app

Part 3: Rule-Based Evaluators

The evaluators.py file checks:

  • Expected keywords
  • Prohibited phrases
  • Required sections

These are simple checks, but they are useful.

They catch obvious failures.

Part 4: Cost Tracker

The cost_tracker.py file estimates tokens and cost.

It uses a rough character-to-token estimate.

This is not exact billing.

It is a learning tool that helps you think about cost.

Part 5: Evaluation Runner

The eval_runner.py file runs all test cases.

For each case, it:

  1. Starts a timer
  2. Calls the assistant
  3. Scores the output
  4. Estimates cost
  5. Stores the result

Part 6: Report Writer

The report_writer.py file saves a Markdown report.

This report helps you compare runs over time.

If you change a prompt, you can rerun evaluation and compare results.

11.25 How to Improve Failed Cases

Suppose a test fails because the answer did not mention “retrieval.”

The issue might be:

missing_keyword:retrieval

Possible fixes:

Fix the System Prompt

Add:

When explaining RAG, mention retrieval and generation clearly.

Fix the User Prompt

Change:

Explain RAG.

to:

Explain RAG and include the roles of retrieval and generation.

Add Required Sections

For important responses, ask for:

Definition:
How it works:
Example:
Limitations:

Improve the Evaluation Case

Maybe the keyword check is too strict.

For example, the model might say:

finding relevant context

instead of:

retrieval

In that case, you can add alternative acceptable keywords.

Evaluation itself needs iteration.

11.26 Evaluating RAG Apps

RAG apps need special evaluation.

Do not only evaluate the final answer.

Evaluate retrieval too.

A RAG evaluation should check:

Was the right chunk retrieved?
Did the answer use the retrieved context?
Did the answer cite the source?
Did the assistant say "not found" when the answer was missing?
Did the answer avoid outside knowledge?

RAG Debugging Table

ProblemLikely CauseFix
Wrong answerWrong chunks retrievedInspect retrieval results
Answer is vagueChunks too broadImprove chunking
Answer invents factsPrompt too looseAdd “use only context” rule
No source shownMetadata missingStore page/source metadata
Slow retrievalToo many chunksOptimize indexing
Not found too oftenRetrieval too strictIncrease results or improve chunking
Irrelevant contextPoor query or embeddingsImprove query and documents

Simple RAG Evaluation Case

{

"id": "refund_policy_answer",
"input": "What is the refund policy?",
"expected_keywords": ["refund", "days"],
"prohibited_phrases": ["I assume", "probably"],
"required_sections": ["Answer", "Source"],
"notes": "The answer should include source information."
}

For strong RAG testing, create a small document with known answers.

Then test answerable and unanswerable questions.

11.27 Evaluating Tool-Using Agents

Tool-using agents need different checks.

Ask:

Did the agent choose the right tool?
Did it pass the right input?
Did the tool return the expected result?
Did the final answer match the tool result?
Did the agent avoid unauthorized tools?
Did risky tools require approval?

A tool agent evaluation should log:

  • User request
  • Selected tool
  • Tool input
  • Tool result
  • Final answer
  • Errors
  • Approval status

Example test case:

{

"id": "calculator_multiplication",
"input": "What is 25 * 4?",
"expected_keywords": ["100"],
"prohibited_phrases": ["I think"],
"required_sections": [],
"notes": "The calculator tool should be used."
}

For tool agents, the most important thing is not only the answer.

It is whether the correct tool was used safely.

11.28 Evaluating Memory Assistants

Memory assistants need privacy and relevance tests.

Ask:

Does the assistant use memory only when relevant?
Can the user inspect memory?
Can the user delete memory?
Does the assistant avoid storing secrets?
Does the assistant avoid exposing private memory unnecessarily?

Test cases:

/remember I prefer short answers.

Then:

Explain RAG.

Expected behavior:

The answer should be concise.

Risky test:

/remember My password is abc123.

Expected behavior:

The assistant should refuse or warn.

Memory evaluation is not only about usefulness.

It is also about privacy.

11.29 Evaluating Workflow Agents

Workflow agents need process-level evaluation.

For Chapter 8’s freelance agent, evaluate:

Did it identify the client goal?
Did it list deliverables?
Did it ask clarifying questions?
Did it avoid inventing price?
Did it avoid inventing deadline?
Did it include human review?

A workflow output may have several sections.

So required-section checks are useful.

Example:

{

"id": "freelance_proposal_workflow",
"input": "I need a website for my coaching business.",
"expected_keywords": ["website", "clarifying"],
"prohibited_phrases": ["guarantee", "$999", "delivered tomorrow"],
"required_sections": ["Project Analysis", "Proposal Draft", "Human Review"],
"notes": "The workflow should not invent price or deadline."
}

11.30 Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflows

Multi-agent workflows need stage-by-stage evaluation.

Do not only evaluate the final output.

Evaluate:

  • Planner output
  • Researcher notes
  • Writer draft
  • Reviewer feedback
  • Final revised brief

For Chapter 9, check:

Did the planner create useful questions?
Did the researcher mark claims needing verification?
Did the writer avoid fake citations?
Did the reviewer identify weak claims?
Did the final brief improve?

A common multi-agent failure is error amplification.

One step invents a claim.

The next step polishes it.

The final result sounds even more convincing.

That is why saved intermediate outputs matter.

11.31 Monitoring Basics

Testing happens before or during development.

Monitoring happens while the app is being used.

For beginner projects, monitoring can be simple.

Track:

  • Number of requests
  • Errors
  • Latency
  • Model calls
  • Estimated cost
  • Guardrail triggers
  • Tool calls
  • Failed evaluations
  • User feedback

A simple log line might look like:

2026-05-23T14:30:00 - request_id=abc123 - status=success - latency=1.84s - cost=$0.000061

For production systems, monitoring can become more advanced.

But the beginner habit is simple:

Do not let failures disappear silently.

11.32 Logging Best Practices

Logs are useful, but they can also create privacy risks.

Follow these rules.

Do Log

  • Timestamps
  • Error types
  • Tool names
  • Latency
  • Cost estimates
  • Case IDs
  • Pass/fail status
  • Non-sensitive metadata

Do Not Log Carelessly

  • API keys
  • Passwords
  • Private user data
  • Full confidential documents
  • Payment details
  • Sensitive memory
  • Client secrets

For local learning projects, simple logs are fine.

For client work, logging needs careful design.

11.33 Cost Control

AI apps can become expensive if you are not careful.

Cost can increase because of:

  • Long prompts
  • Large document chunks
  • Too many retrieved results
  • Multi-agent workflows
  • Repeated retries
  • Running evaluations too often
  • Using expensive models for simple tasks
  • Sending full conversation history every time

Cost control techniques:

Use smaller models for simple tasks.
Retrieve only relevant context.
Limit output length.
Cache repeated results.
Avoid unnecessary agent loops.
Batch evaluations carefully.
Track call counts.
Use normal Python when AI is not needed.

The most important question:

Does this step need an LLM?

If not, use normal code.

11.34 Latency Control

Latency means how long the user waits.

An app can be accurate but still frustrating if it is too slow.

Latency increases when:

  • Prompts are long
  • Outputs are long
  • Multiple model calls run sequentially
  • Tools are slow
  • APIs timeout
  • Retrieval is inefficient
  • Large files are processed every time

Ways to reduce latency:

  • Use shorter prompts
  • Use fewer workflow steps
  • Cache indexed documents
  • Avoid reprocessing PDFs every run
  • Use timeouts
  • Retrieve fewer chunks
  • Use faster models for simple steps
  • Show progress messages for long workflows

In user-facing apps, perception matters.

If a task takes time, show progress.

11.35 Evaluation Dataset Growth

Start with a small evaluation set.

Then grow it as you find failures.

A good evaluation dataset includes:

Easy cases
Normal cases
Edge cases
Risky cases
Unanswerable cases
Format-specific cases
Long-input cases
Ambiguous cases

For a RAG app, include:

Questions answered directly in the document
Questions answered indirectly
Questions not answered at all
Questions requiring source citation
Questions with similar wording but different meaning

For a tool agent, include:

Correct tool cases
Wrong-tool traps
Unsafe tool requests
Messy tool inputs
API failure cases

Your evaluation dataset becomes your quality memory.

Every bug you find should become a future test case.

11.38 Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Testing Only One Prompt

One good response does not prove the app is reliable.

Create a test set.

Mistake 2: Testing Only Happy Paths

Include vague, risky, and unanswerable inputs.

Mistake 3: Ignoring Retrieval

For RAG apps, always inspect retrieved chunks.

Mistake 4: Ignoring Cost

Multi-agent workflows can multiply cost quickly.

Track call counts and estimated usage.

Mistake 5: Ignoring Latency

A slow app may feel broken even when it is correct.

Mistake 6: Using Exact Match Too Often

AI output varies.

Use keyword, section, and meaning-based checks when appropriate.

Mistake 7: Not Saving Reports

If you do not save results, you cannot compare improvements.

Mistake 8: Not Turning Bugs Into Tests

Every failure should become a future evaluation case.

11.39 Best Practices

Create evaluation cases early.

Separate code tests from AI evaluations.

Test normal, edge, risky, and unanswerable cases.

Evaluate retrieval separately from generation.

Track latency.

Estimate cost.

Save reports.

Review failed outputs manually.

Add guardrail tests.

Use smaller models when possible.

Use normal Python where possible.

Turn discovered failures into new test cases.
